sections.title: Defining psychology and its history
sections.html:
Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes. Each part of that definition matters:

  • Science: psychologists use systematic methods to observe, describe, predict and explain.
  • Behaviour: everything we do that can be directly observed (talking, smiling, running).
  • Mental processes: thoughts, feelings and motives that cannot be seen directly but are still studied.

The scientific attitude rests on four habits: critical thinking (reflecting deeply and asking questions), scepticism (challenging things that are taken as fact), objectivity (relying on evidence, not feelings) and curiosity.

Psychology is not only the study of mental illness. Freud's view focused on disorder, but positive psychology studies strengths, happiness and what makes life worth living.

Roots of psychology

Psychology grew out of Western philosophy (questions about the mind) and physiology (how the body works).

WhoSchoolBig ideaMethod
Wilhelm Wundt (1832–1920)StructuralismFind the basic structures (elements) of the mind. In 1879 he opened the first psychology laboratory in Leipzig and timed the lag between hearing a sound and responding, showing mental processes can be measured.Introspection: systematic, detailed self-reports of one's own experience
William JamesFunctionalismAsk what the mind is for. The mind is flexible and always changing (a stream of consciousness); thought exists because it helps us adapt.Observation of how the mind helps us adapt
Charles DarwinEvolutionNatural selection: organisms best adapted to their environment survive and reproduce, passing on helpful traits; competition for food and shelter, and changes in the environment, shape evolution.Comparative observation

Remember: structuralism asks what the mind is made of; functionalism asks why it works the way it does.

sections.title: Contemporary approaches to psychology
sections.html:
Seven approaches look at the same behaviour from different angles. They are complementary, not rivals: together they give a fuller picture.

ApproachFocusKey names
BiologicalThe brain and nervous system. Thoughts and emotions have a physical basis. Neuroscience studies the structure, function, development, genetics and biochemistry of the nervous system.—
BehaviouralEnvironmental causes of observable behaviour; rejects studying thought processes.John Watson, B. F. Skinner
PsychodynamicUnconscious thought, conflict between biological drives and society's demands, early childhood family experiences.Sigmund Freud (psychoanalysis)
HumanisticPositive human qualities, the capacity for positive growth, free will.Carl Rogers, Abraham Maslow
CognitiveThe mental processes involved in knowing: how we take in, interpret, store and use information (information processing).—
EvolutionaryAdaptation, reproduction and natural selection as explanations of behaviour.David Buss, Leda Cosmides
SocioculturalHow social and cultural environments shape behaviour; compares ethnic and cultural groups within and across countries.—

Exam tip: when asked to "compare approaches", take one behaviour (say, aggression) and show what each approach would look at: brain chemistry, rewards, childhood conflict, choice, thoughts, survival value, culture.

sections.title: Careers, specialisations and the mind–body link
sections.html:
Psychologists work in three broad kinds of job: practice/applied, research and teaching, in universities, clinics, private practice, industry and schools.

Areas of specialisation

  • Physiological psychology / behavioural neuroscience; sensation and perception; learning; cognitive psychology
  • Developmental; motivation and emotion; psychology of women and gender; personality; social psychology
  • Industrial/organisational; clinical and counselling; health psychology
  • Also: community, school and educational, environmental, forensic, sport and cross-cultural psychology

Psychology in other fields

  • Business: market research, human resources, advertising and sales use psychology directly. Business psychology is an applied science that studies people, workplaces and organisations to make them more effective and to balance their competing needs.
  • Law: knowledge of adaptive and maladaptive behaviour, of how decisions are made, and of assessment. Parole and probation officers assess whether an offender can live in society without posing a threat.
  • Education: educational psychology studies how people learn and retain information: student outcomes, instruction, individual differences, gifted learners and learning disabilities.

Health and wellness: the mind–body connection is a two-way street. The mind affects the body (stress can make you ill) and the body affects the mind (illness or exercise changes mood).

sections.title: The scientific method
sections.html:
Science is a method: it is not what you study but how you study it.

The scientific method usually starts from a theory: a broad idea or set of related ideas that explains observations and predicts future ones. It then runs through five steps.

  1. Observe a phenomenon. What scientists study are variables: anything that can change (e.g. happiness).
  2. Formulate hypotheses and predictions. A hypothesis is a testable prediction derived logically from a theory. It is not a fact until research supports it.
  3. Test through empirical research: design a study, choose participants and operationally define the variables, collect data and analyse it with statistics.
  4. Draw conclusions from the analysis. A finding is reliable when the study has been replicated again and again with similar results.
  5. Evaluate the theory. Evaluation never ends: findings are published in journals and presented at conferences, where others question them. Meta-analysis combines the results of many studies of one topic to see whether an effect is consistent and how strong it is.

Operational definitions

An operational definition states exactly how a variable will be observed and measured. It removes grey areas. For example, happiness could be defined as a score on the Satisfaction with Life Scale (five ratings added and divided by 5), or by life satisfaction, facial expressions and so on.

sections.title: Descriptive, correlational and experimental research
sections.html:
TypeGoalMethodsLimits
DescriptiveDescribe a phenomenon: what it is, how often, where and whenObservation (must be systematic: know what, who, where, when and how); surveys and interviews (self-reported attitudes; open-ended or structured questions); case studies (in-depth look at one person, family or group)Cannot explain why; surveys suffer from socially desirable answers; a case may not generalise
CorrelationalIdentify relationships: how two variables change togetherMeasure variables and compute the correlation coefficient r (−1.00 to +1.00); plot scatter plotsCorrelation does not equal causation; the third variable problem
ExperimentalDetermine causationManipulate the independent variable, measure the dependent variable; random assignment to experimental and control groupsValidity threats, bias, artificial settings

Correlation in detail

  • The number in r gives strength (closer to ±1 is stronger); the sign gives direction.
  • Positive: both move in the same direction. Negative: one rises as the other falls.
  • Even without showing cause, correlations allow prediction, and let us study variables that cannot or should not be manipulated (e.g. the effects of alcohol before birth).
  • A longitudinal design measures the same variables in several waves over time, which hints at causal direction but still does not prove it.

Experiments in detail

  • An experiment is a carefully regulated procedure in which the researcher manipulates one or more variables believed to influence another.
  • Independent variable (IV): what the experimenter changes, the potential cause (e.g. playing a violent video game or not). Dependent variable (DV): the outcome measured, the effect (e.g. aggression).
  • Experimental group gets the manipulation; the control group is treated the same in every way except the IV, giving a comparison.
  • Because of random assignment, the only systematic difference between the groups is the IV, so differences in the DV can be put down to it.
  • Quasi-experimental designs compare groups that already differ (soldiers who went to war and those who did not; children whose school burned down) without random assignment.

Reliability, validity and bias

  • Reliable: findings replicate and stand the test of time. A reliable finding is not necessarily valid.
  • Validity: the degree to which a study measures what it intends to. External validity: do results generalise to the real world? Internal validity: are changes in the DV really caused by the IV, free of bias and logical errors?
  • Experimenter bias: the researcher's expectations influence the outcome. Demand characteristics: cues that tell participants how they are expected to behave.
  • Research participant bias: participants act how they think they should. Placebo effect: participants' expectations produce an outcome without any real manipulation.
  • Control both with a double-blind experiment: neither experimenter nor participant knows who is in which group.

Baumeister found high self-esteem led to aggression; Donnellan and Trzesniewski found low self-esteem did. Differences in setting (lab-only aggression) and in the type of self-esteem measured can explain conflicting results. That is why evaluation never stops.

sections.title: Samples, settings and statistics
sections.html:
Samples

  • Population: the whole group the researcher wants to draw conclusions about. Sample: the subset actually studied.
  • Representative sample: has the same characteristics as the population (the opposite of a biased sample). Random sample: every member has an equal chance of being chosen.

Settings

Any of the three research types can happen in any setting: the setting does not decide the design.

  • Laboratory: controlled, with complex real-world factors removed. Drawbacks: participants know they are studied; the setting is unnatural; some behaviour is hard to study there; university volunteers may not represent the population.
  • Natural setting: naturalistic observation of behaviour in real-world situations.

Statistics

KindPurposeExamples
Descriptive statisticsDescribe and summarise data; show the big pictureCentral tendency: mean (ΣX ÷ N), median (middle score), mode (most frequent). Dispersion: range (highest − lowest), standard deviation (average spread around the mean)
Inferential statisticsDraw conclusions: does the data support the hypothesis, or could the difference be chance?A difference is statistically significant when p < 0.05 (less than 5 in 100 chance it is due to chance); stricter p < 0.01

Try it: scores 2, 4, 4, 6, 9. Mean = 25 ÷ 5 = 5; median = 4; mode = 4; range = 9 − 2 = 7. A smaller standard deviation would mean the scores cluster closer to the mean.

sections.title: Research ethics and being a wise consumer
sections.html:
Ethics

Researchers must run studies ethically and try to overcome their own biases. Participants have rights, protected by an Institutional Review Board (IRB) and the APA guidelines:

  • Informed consent: participants know what they are agreeing to and may withdraw.
  • Confidentiality: data are kept private and anonymous.
  • Debriefing: after the study, participants are told its purpose and methods.
  • Deception: allowed only when needed and harmless, and always followed by debriefing.

Animal research

Animal research has benefited humans. About 5% of researchers use animals, and rats and mice are used about 90% of the time. Standards of care cover housing, feeding, and psychological and physical well-being.

A wise consumer is sceptical yet open-minded

  • Be careful applying group trends to one individual.
  • Avoid overgeneralising from a small or unrepresentative sample.
  • Look for converging evidence from more than one study.
  • Question causal claims, especially from correlational research.
  • Consider the source (tabloids vs journals) and watch for pseudoscience.

Expressive writing and health: survivors of a suicide death talked less about the loss and had poorer health than survivors of an accidental death. This led to studies in which people assigned to write about a trauma later had better physical health.

sections.title: The nervous system and its divisions
sections.html:
The nervous system is the body's electrochemical communication system, made of billions of communicating cells. Its purpose is to direct behaviour. Neuroscience is the field that studies it.

Four characteristics

  • Complexity: billions of nerve cells work together so we can do a huge range of things.
  • Integration: the brain pulls together information from the environment; each nerve cell communicates with about ten thousand others.
  • Adaptability (plasticity): a vast capacity for modification and change as the world changes.
  • Electrochemical transmission: electrical impulses and chemical messengers make the brain an information-processing system.

Pathways

  • Afferent nerves carry information to the spinal cord and brain (sensory input). Efferent nerves carry it from the brain to the body and muscles. Memory aid: Afferent Arrives, Efferent Exits.
  • Neural networks integrate sensory input and motor output. Reading aloud: input from the eyes passes through networks that turn marks into letters, words and meanings; some is stored, some is sent on to the tongue and lips.

Divisions

DivisionMade ofJob
Central nervous system (CNS)Brain and spinal cordProcesses information and issues commands
Peripheral nervous system (PNS)Nerves connecting the CNS to the rest of the bodyBrings information to and from the CNS; carries out its commands
↳ Somatic nervous systemPart of the PNSCarries information from skin and muscles to the CNS (pain, temperature) and voluntary movement
↳ Autonomic nervous systemPart of the PNSMessages to and from internal organs: breathing, heart rate, digestion
  ↳ SympatheticPart of the autonomic systemArouses: prepares the body for a stressful situation (fight or flight)
  ↳ ParasympatheticPart of the autonomic systemCalms the body down afterwards

sections.title: Neurons, the neural impulse and neurotransmitters
sections.html:
Two kinds of cell

  • Neurons: about 100 billion nerve cells that handle information processing. Mirror neurons (primates and humans) fire both when we perform an action and when we watch someone else do it; they play a role in imitation, empathy and understanding others.
  • Glial cells: support and nourish neurons and keep them running smoothly. There are about as many glia as neurons, but neurons do most of the information processing.

Structure of a neuron

  • Cell body: contains the nucleus, which makes what the neuron needs for growth and maintenance.
  • Dendrites: receive information and pass it to the cell body.
  • Axon: carries information away from the cell body to other cells.
  • Myelin sheath: fatty layer around the axon that protects and insulates it and speeds up nerve impulses. Breakdown of myelin causes multiple sclerosis.

The neural impulse

  1. The axon membrane has ion channels; it is semi-permeable. Positive ions (sodium, potassium) and negative ions (chloride and others) float inside and outside.
  2. At rest the channels are closed: the inside is negative, the outside positive. This resting potential (about −60 to −75 mV) means the membrane is polarised.
  3. When the neuron fires, sodium channels open, positive ions rush in and the axon depolarises. Potassium channels then open, positive ions flow out, and the normal charge returns.
  4. This impulse travelling down the axon is the action potential; the neuron is said to be firing.
  5. All-or-none principle: once the impulse reaches threshold, it fires all the way down the axon at full strength and cannot be stopped.

Synaptic transmission

  1. The synapse (synaptic gap) is the tiny space between one neuron's axon and the next neuron's dendrites. The electrical signal must become a chemical one to cross it.
  2. Axon fibres end in terminal buttons, whose synaptic vesicles store neurotransmitters.
  3. The impulse triggers release of neurotransmitters into the gap. They fit receptor sites on the dendrite like a key in a lock.
  4. Afterwards, the neurotransmitter is used up or reabsorbed by the sending axon: reuptake.
  5. Some neurotransmitters excite (make the next neuron fire); others inhibit.
NeurotransmitterRoleLinked to
Acetylcholine (ACh)Muscle action, learning, memoryBlack widow venom ↑ ACh; Botox ↓ ACh; Alzheimer's: ↓ ACh
GABAInhibitory; keeps firing preciseAnxiety: ↓ GABA
GlutamateExcitatory; learning and memoryMany psychological disorders
NorepinephrineStress; regulates sleep with AChStress and mania ↑; depression ↓
DopamineVoluntary movement, reward anticipationStimulant drugs activate it; Parkinson's ↓; schizophrenia ↑
SerotoninSleep, mood, attention, learningDepression ↓; Prozac raises it by slowing reuptake
EndorphinsNatural opiates: dull pain, raise pleasure—
OxytocinHormone and neurotransmitter: lactation, attachment and emotional bonds—

Drugs and synapses: an agonist mimics or boosts a neurotransmitter's effect; an antagonist blocks it.

sections.title: Studying the brain and its structures
sections.html:
Methods

MethodWhat it does
Brain lesioningStudies damage from injury or disease; in animals, tissue is removed, lasered or destroyed by drugs to see the effect on behaviour
EEG (electroencephalograph)Scalp electrodes record brain-wave activity; used for brain damage and epilepsy
Single-unit recordingA probe in or near one neuron records its electrical activity
CT scanX-rays build a 3-D image; shows where damage is and how large
PET scanMeasures glucose use (neurons burn glucose), showing activity levels
MRIMagnetic field and radio waves give clear pictures of structure; shows how experience changes structure but not function
fMRIShows the brain while it is working
TMS (transcranial magnetic stimulation)Brief pulses create a temporary 'virtual lesion'; if behaviour is disrupted, that area is linked to it, allowing causal inferences

How the brain develops and is organised

The nervous system starts as a hollow tube; about three weeks after conception its cells become neurons and form the hindbrain, midbrain and forebrain.

RegionStructureFunction
HindbrainMedullaBreathing, reflexes
CerebellumMotor coordination of arm and leg movements
PonsSleep and arousal
Brain stemHouses medulla and pons; survival functions: breathing, heartbeat, blood pressure
Midbrain—Relays information between brain and eyes and ears
Reticular formationWalking, sleeping, turning towards a noise
Substantia nigraDamaged in Parkinson's: rigidity, tremors, poor movement
ForebrainLimbic system: amygdalaRecognising things needed for survival; emotional awareness and expression
Limbic system: hippocampusForming and recalling memories
ThalamusRelay station for sensory information
Basal gangliaCoordinating voluntary movement
HypothalamusEating, drinking, sex; internal state; emotion, stress and reward

Brain stem, cerebellum and cerebral cortex are found across species; each species' brain is adapted to its environment.

sections.title: The cerebral cortex and the two hemispheres
sections.html:
The cerebral cortex is the outer layer of the forebrain and controls the highest mental functions such as thinking and planning. Its outermost part is the neocortex.

LobeFunctions
OccipitalVision: the eyes only carry information; it is interpreted here
TemporalHearing, language processing, memory; contains the fusiform face area (right temporal lobe)
FrontalIntelligence, personality, voluntary muscles; contains the motor cortex
ParietalSpatial location, attention, motor control; contains the somatosensory cortex

Phineas Gage (1823–1860): an iron rod passed through his head and destroyed much of his left frontal lobe. His personality changed so much that friends said he was "no longer Gage", showing the frontal lobe's role in personality.

  • Prosopagnosia: inability to recognise faces but not other objects, which points to a face area, the fusiform face area.
  • Somatosensory cortex (parietal): body sensations. Motor cortex (frontal): voluntary movement. Both have point-to-point mapping: Wilder Penfield stimulated spots and specific body parts responded.
  • Association cortex (75% of the cortex, mostly in the frontal lobes): integrates sensory and motor information for thinking and problem solving. Damage harms planning (executive functions).

Hemispheres

Left hemisphereRight hemisphere
Language: words, numbers, grammar; locating objectsNon-verbal: spatial perception, recognising faces, emotion
Broca's area damage: trouble speaking; Wernicke's area damage: trouble understanding speech (both are aphasias)Meanings of stories, tone of voice, melodies
Receives information from the right side of the bodyReceives information from the left side of the body

Split-brain research: the corpus callosum is a bundle of axons linking the hemispheres. When it is cut (as in W. J., treated for epilepsy), the halves cannot share information, so something stored on one side seems "lost" to the other: in effect two separate minds.

sections.title: Endocrine system, plasticity and genetics
sections.html:
Endocrine system

A set of glands that regulate the body by releasing hormones (chemical messengers) into the bloodstream. It is slower than the nervous system and interconnected with it.

GlandRole
PituitaryControls growth and regulates other glands (the 'master gland')
AdrenalMood, energy and coping with stress; secretes epinephrine and norepinephrine
PancreasDigestive and endocrine; insulin regulates metabolism and body weight
ThyroidRate of energy use, protein making, sensitivity to other hormones, metabolism and calcium balance
Ovaries and testesHormones for sexual development and reproduction

Brain damage, plasticity and repair

Recovery depends on the person's age and the extent of the damage. Repair mechanisms: collateral sprouting (axons of healthy neurons grow new branches), substitution of function (another area takes over), neurogenesis (new neurons) and brain tissue grafts.

Genetics and behaviour

  • Dominant–recessive principle: a dominant gene overrides a recessive one.
  • Molecular genetics: manipulating genes to see their effect on behaviour. Selective breeding: breeding organisms for how much of a trait they show.
  • Behaviour genetics: how much heredity influences behaviour. Twin studies compare identical with fraternal twins.
  • Genotype: genetic heritage. Phenotype: observable characteristics, shaped by genes and environment. Gene expression is itself influenced by the environment.

Health: stressors are events that threaten us or tax our coping; stress is our response. Acute and chronic stress have different causes and effects on the body.

sections.title: What learning is, and classical conditioning
sections.html:
Learning is a systematic, relatively permanent change in behaviour that occurs through experience. Behaviourism studies learning through observable behaviour only, leaving out thinking, wishing and hoping.

  • Associative learning (conditioning): an association is made between two events. Two kinds: classical and operant conditioning.
  • Observational learning: watching and imitating someone else; relies on attention, remembering and recall.

Pavlov's discovery

Ivan Pavlov, a Russian physiologist studying digestion, noticed that his dogs salivated not only to meat powder but also to the sight of it, the person who brought it and the sound of the door. Their behaviour had unlearned parts (reflexes) and learned parts.

Classical conditioning explains involuntary behaviour: a neutral stimulus becomes associated with a meaningful stimulus and comes to produce a similar response.

TermMeaningPavlov's dogs
Unconditioned stimulus (UCS)Produces a response without learningMeat powder
Unconditioned response (UCR)Unlearned response to the UCSSalivating to the food
Neutral stimulus (NS)Produces no response of interest before conditioningBell, before pairing
Conditioned stimulus (CS)The former NS, after pairing with the UCSBell, after pairing
Conditioned response (CR)Learned response to the CSSalivating to the bell

Acquisition and its two conditions

Acquisition is learning the association: UCS → UCR; NS paired with UCS; after pairings NS alone → CR, so NS has become a CS. It needs contiguity (CS and UCS close in time) and contingency (the CS reliably signals that the UCS is coming).

Other processes

  • Generalisation: a similar new stimulus produces a similar response. Discrimination: responding to some stimuli but not others (learned by presenting other stimuli without the UCS).
  • Extinction: the CR weakens when the CS is presented without the UCS (bell, no food, no saliva).
  • Spontaneous recovery: the CR comes back after a delay with no new learning (the dog salivates again next day; feelings for an ex returning).
  • Renewal: the CR returns when the organism is placed in a new context.

Applications

  • Phobias: Watson and Rayner (1920) paired a white rat (CS) with a loud noise (UCS) until Little Albert feared the rat.
  • Counterconditioning: pair the CS with a new, incompatible response; aversive conditioning is one technique.
  • Also: the placebo effect, immune and endocrine responses, taste aversion, advertising and drug habituation.

sections.title: Operant conditioning, reinforcement and punishment
sections.html:
Operant (instrumental) conditioning, developed by B. F. Skinner, is associative learning in which the consequences of a voluntary behaviour change how likely it is to happen again. Contingency matters here too.

  • Thorndike's law of effect: consequences strengthen or weaken a stimulus–response connection (his puzzle-box cats).
  • Shaping: rewarding closer and closer approximations of the desired behaviour.
Stimulus added (+)Stimulus removed (−)
Increase behaviour (reinforcement)Positive reinforcement: something pleasant added (praise for homework)Negative reinforcement: something unpleasant removed (seatbelt beep stops when you buckle up)
Decrease behaviour (punishment)Positive punishment: something unpleasant added (a scolding)Negative punishment: something pleasant removed (phone taken away)

Negative reinforcement is not punishment. "Negative" means something is taken away; reinforcement always increases behaviour.

  • Avoidance learning: a response lets you avoid an unpleasant stimulus. Learned helplessness: learning you have no control over negative outcomes, so you stop trying.
  • Primary reinforcers are innately satisfying (food, water). Secondary reinforcers become satisfying through association (money, grades).
  • Generalisation, discrimination, extinction and spontaneous recovery work here too: behaviour fades when reinforcement stops.

Schedules of reinforcement

Continuous: reinforce every time (fast learning, fast extinction). Partial: reinforce some of the time.

Fixed (predictable)Variable (unpredictable)
Ratio (number of responses)FR: after a set number (paid per 10 items made)VR: after an unpredictable number (gambling)
Interval (time passed)FI: first response after a set time (weekly test)VI: first response after an unpredictable time (fishing, pop quizzes)

Punishment controversy and timing

Corporal punishment is used by 70–90% of US parents, but correlational research links it to problems, which raises the question of whether physical punishment is ever necessary. Consequences work best when immediate. Applied behaviour analysis (behaviour modification) uses operant principles to change behaviour in real life.

sections.title: Observational learning and cognitive factors
sections.html:
Observational learning (Bandura)

Learning by watching and imitating a model (modelling). Bandura's four processes:

  1. Attention: notice what the model does or says.
  2. Retention: code the behaviour and keep it in memory.
  3. Motor reproduction: be physically able to perform it.
  4. Reinforcement: have an incentive to actually do it.

Cognition in learning

  • Tolman's purposive behaviour: behaviour is goal-directed; organisms form expectancies from experience.
  • Cognitive map: a mental representation of physical space.
  • Latent learning: learning that happens without reinforcement and only shows later when there is a reason to use it (you learn where buildings are on your daily route but only show it when you need one).
  • Insight learning (Wolfgang Köhler): a sudden understanding of a problem's solution, as if it "pops" into your head.

sections.title: Biological, cultural and psychological factors in learning
sections.html:
• Biological constraints: an organism's body allows some behaviours and blocks others.
  • Instinctive drift: animals slip back into instinctive behaviour that interferes with what they were trained to do.
  • Preparedness: a biological readiness to learn some things more easily than others. Taste aversion needs only one pairing of food and sickness for long-lasting learning.
  • Culture shapes how conditioning and observational learning are used, and what is learned: we cannot learn about what we never experience.
  • Psychological constraints: mindset. A fixed mindset believes ability cannot change; a growth mindset believes it can be developed, and learns more.

sections.title: Cognition, concepts and problem solving
sections.html:
Cognition is how information is processed and manipulated when remembering, thinking and knowing. In the cognitive revolution of the 1950s psychology turned back to the mind, using the computer as an analogy for the brain and giving rise to artificial intelligence (AI).

Thinking is mentally manipulating information: forming concepts, solving problems, making decisions and reflecting critically or creatively.

Concepts

Concepts are mental categories that group objects, events and characteristics (dogs, insects, people). They matter because they let us generalise, associate experiences and objects, aid memory (no reinventing the wheel), and give clues about how to react.

The prototype model: we compare each new case to an ideal example (prototype). Concepts list properties members tend to have, not ones they must have, so exceptions fit: a three-legged dog is still a dog; a penguin is a bird though it cannot fly.

Problem solving

Finding a way to reach a goal when the solution is not readily available.

  1. Find and frame the problem.
  2. Develop strategies: subgoals (intermediate goals), algorithms (step-by-step procedures that guarantee an answer), heuristics (shortcuts that suggest but do not guarantee an answer).
  3. Evaluate solutions.
  4. Rethink and redefine problems and solutions over time.

Obstacles: fixation (sticking to a strategy that worked before) and functional fixedness (seeing an object only in its usual use, e.g. not thinking of a coin as a screwdriver).

sections.title: Reasoning, decision making, and critical and creative thinking
sections.html:
Reasoning

InductiveDeductive
DirectionBottom-up: specific → generalTop-down: general → specific
Driven byDataLogic
ExampleStudy a sample, then generaliseDerive a hypothesis from a theory

Decision making

Evaluating alternatives and choosing among them to get the best outcome. Two systems: System I (automatic, rapid, heuristic, intuitive) and System II (controlled, slower, effortful, analytical).

BiasWhat happensExample
Confirmation biasLooking only for information that supports our ideasReading only news that agrees with you
Hindsight biasFalsely claiming we predicted an outcome'I knew it all along'
Availability heuristicJudging probability by how easily examples come to mindFearing flying after a recent crash
Base-rate fallacyIgnoring general information about how common something is—
Representativeness heuristicJudging by stereotypesAssuming a woman does not fit engineering

Critical, emotional and creative thinking

  • Critical thinking: reflective, productive thinking that evaluates evidence; helped by mindfulness (alert and present) and open-mindedness.
  • Mood and thinking: bad moods → careful logic; good moods → efficiency, originality and creativity, ignoring irrelevant information.
  • Divergent thinking produces many answers (creative); convergent thinking narrows to one correct answer.
  • Creative thinkers brainstorm, think flexibly and playfully, have inner motivation, are willing to take risks and evaluate their work objectively.

Health: cognitive appraisal shapes stress. Primary appraisal: is this a threat? Secondary appraisal: can I cope? Cognitive reappraisal: rethinking a situation to see it more positively.

sections.title: Intelligence and its measurement
sections.html:
Definitions of intelligence reflect culture. In the US it is often seen as Spearman's g, a general intelligence measured by intelligence tests. Good tests are valid (measure what they claim), reliable (consistent) and standardised (given and scored the same way, with norms).

IQ

  • Binet compared mental age (MA) with chronological age (CA).
  • Stern: IQ = MA ÷ CA × 100. If MA = CA, IQ = 100 (average). A 10-year-old with MA 12 has IQ 120.
  • Scores follow a normal distribution (bell curve) centred on 100.
  • Tests: the Stanford-Binet (from age 2), the WAIS and WISC (Wechsler, 1939) and the Woodcock battery.

Influences on scores

  • Cultural bias: tests can favour one culture. Culture-fair tests such as Raven's Progressive Matrices (about 60 non-verbal items measuring abstract reasoning, or fluid intelligence) try to avoid this.
  • Genetic: heritability is the share of variation in a group explained by genes.
  • Environmental: the Flynn effect, a worldwide rise in IQ scores over generations, too fast to be genetic.

Extremes

  • Giftedness: IQ ≥ 130. Terman found gifted children became socially well-adjusted, successful adults.
  • Intellectual disability: IQ < 70 with deficits in adaptive behaviour (conceptual, social, practical). Causes may be organic (genetic or brain damage) or cultural-familial. Levels: mild, moderate, severe/profound.

Multiple intelligences

  • Sternberg's triarchic theory: analytical (analyse, judge, compare), creative (create, design, imagine) and practical (use, apply) intelligence.
  • Gardner's frames of mind: verbal, mathematical, spatial, bodily-kinaesthetic, musical, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalist, existentialist. Everyone has all of them to different degrees.

sections.title: Language and thought
sections.html:
Language is spoken, written or signed communication based on symbols. All human languages have infinite generativity: the ability to produce endless meaningful sentences.

Rule systemWhat it coversExample
PhonologyThe basic sounds (phonemes)'ch' in chat
MorphologyHow words are formedhelp + ful + ness
SyntaxHow words combine into phrases and sentencesWord order
SemanticsMeaning of words and sentences'Bank' of a river vs a bank for money
PragmaticsUsing language appropriately in contextSpeaking formally to a lecturer

Language and thought

Whorf's linguistic relativity hypothesis: language determines thought. Research suggests language influences thought, and cognition also shapes language: the relationship runs both ways. Popular claims such as "women are more talkative" are tested rather than assumed.

Influences on language

  • Biological: language universals shared by all languages; left-hemisphere specialisation (Broca's and Wernicke's areas).
  • Environmental: the behavioural view treats language as a learned skill; exposure matters, as shown by Genie, who was isolated as a child and never fully learned grammar.
  • Sensitive periods: adults learning a second language struggle more with new sounds (accent) and grammar than with new vocabulary.

sections.title: Studying development, prenatal and infant growth
sections.html:
Development is the pattern of continuity and change across the lifespan, on three levels: physical, cognitive and socioemotional processes.

Research designs

  • Cross-sectional: compare different age groups at one time. Quick, but open to cohort effects (differences due to the era a group grew up in, not age).
  • Longitudinal: follow the same people over time. Shows real change but is slow and costly.

Nature, nurture and the developer

Nature is biological inheritance; nurture is environmental experience. People are also active developers: they can seek out good experiences and go beyond what life has given them. Resilience, the ability to recover from or adapt to difficult times, lets children who face hardship become capable adults.

Prenatal development

PeriodTimingWhat happens
GerminalWeeks 1–2Conception: sperm and ovum form a zygote with 23 chromosomes from each parent
EmbryonicWeeks 3–8Organs and basic structures form
FetalMonths 2–9Growth and maturing of organs and systems

Teratogens are agents that cause birth defects: nicotine, alcohol, STIs. Fetal alcohol syndrome causes physical and intellectual abnormalities. Effects depend on the timing of exposure (a developing organ is most vulnerable), genetic characteristics and the postnatal environment.

Infancy

  • Reflexes are genetically wired survival behaviours. Some persist for life (coughing, blinking, yawning); others, like grasping, disappear with neurological development around 6 months.
  • By 12 months most infants sit, stand, climb and walk. Preferential looking studies show infants perceive faces and link sights with sounds.
  • Brain: myelination begins before birth and continues after; synaptic connections increase dramatically in childhood.

sections.title: Piaget's theory of cognitive development
sections.html:
Jean Piaget (1896–1980): children actively construct their understanding of the world using:

  • Schemas: frameworks that organise information.
  • Assimilation: fitting new information into an existing schema (calling a cow a "big dog").
  • Accommodation: changing a schema to fit new information (learning cows are different).
StageAgeKey features
SensorimotorBirth–2Knowledge through senses and movement; develops object permanence (objects exist when out of sight)
Preoperational2–7Symbolic thinking (words, images, drawings); intuitive rather than logical reasoning; egocentrism
Concrete operational7–11Logical reasoning about concrete things; conservation (amount stays the same despite a change in shape); classification
Formal operational11–15 onwardsAbstract and idealistic thought; hypothetical-deductive reasoning

Evaluating Piaget

  • Infants know objects still exist as early as 4 months, earlier than Piaget thought.
  • Too much stress on grand stages, too little on small, precise problem-solving steps.
  • He underplayed culture: whether children master conservation depends partly on whether their culture gives them practice.

sections.title: Temperament, attachment, Erikson, parenting and moral development
sections.html:
Temperament

A person's characteristic style of responding. Chess and Thomas found three clusters: easy, difficult and slow-to-warm-up. Another view adds effortful control (self-regulation), inhibition (shyness in unfamiliar situations) and negative affectivity (easily frustrated or sad).

Attachment

The close emotional bond between infant and caregiver, a foundation for later relationships.

  • Harlow: infant monkeys spent far more time with a soft cloth "mother" than a wire one, even when only the wire mother gave milk. Contact comfort matters more than feeding.
  • Ainsworth's Strange Situation: the caregiver leaves the infant with a stranger and returns; the infant's reaction shows secure or insecure attachment. Criticism: it ignores cultures where infants are attached to many people.

Erikson's eight psychosocial stages

Development is lifelong; each stage poses a crisis to resolve, leading to competence or weakness.

StageAgeCrisis
1InfancyTrust vs mistrust
2ToddlerAutonomy vs shame and doubt
3Early childhoodInitiative vs guilt
4Middle childhoodIndustry vs inferiority
5AdolescenceIdentity vs identity confusion
6Early adulthoodIntimacy vs isolation
7Middle adulthoodGenerativity vs stagnation
8Late adulthoodIntegrity vs despair

Parenting styles

StyleParents are…Linked to in children
AuthoritarianControlling and punitiveLittle initiative, poor communication, social incompetence
AuthoritativeEncourage independence with limits; collaborativeSocial competence, responsibility, self-reliance (best outcomes)
NeglectfulUninvolvedSocial incompetence, poor self-control
PermissiveInvolved but set few limitsPoor social competence, little respect for others, poor self-control

Kohlberg's moral development

  1. Preconventional: behaviour guided by punishments and rewards.
  2. Conventional: follows standards learned from parents and society.
  3. Postconventional: values, rights and principles the person has reasoned through and accepts.

Parenting that builds morality: warm rather than harsh, reasoning during discipline, helping the child take others' perspectives, involving the child in decisions, and modelling moral behaviour.

sections.title: Adolescence
sections.html:
Adolescence runs from about 10–12 to 18–21 years: a time of evaluation, decision making and commitment. Competence depends on quality education, community support, access to good jobs and especially caring adults.

Physical development

Puberty brings rapid skeletal and sexual maturation. Testosterone (boys): genital development, height, voice change. Estradiol (girls): breast, uterine and skeletal development.

The adolescent brain

The amygdala (emotion) develops early; the prefrontal cortex (reasoning, decisions, controlling risk) develops late. This gap helps explain strong emotions and risk-taking, and some argue it means teenagers who commit violent crimes should not face the death penalty.

Cognitive development

Formal operational thinking appears, along with adolescent egocentrism: believing others are as focused on you as you are, a sense of uniqueness, and a sense of invincibility that feeds risky behaviour.

Identity

Erikson: identity vs identity confusion. Marcia's four statuses use two questions: has the person explored options, and have they committed?

StatusExplored?Committed?
Identity diffusionNoNo
Identity foreclosureNoYes (often parents' choices)
Identity moratoriumYesNo
Identity achievementYesYes

Ethnic identity involves attachment to one's minority group and to the wider culture; biculturalism combines both. Parents act as managers, counsellors and monitors, balancing involvement with room to explore; peer relationships peak in importance.

sections.title: Emerging adulthood, adult development and ageing
sections.html:
Emerging adulthood (18–25)

Part extended adolescence, part trying on adult roles. Five features: identity exploration (love and work), instability, self-focus, feeling "in between", and the age of possibilities.

Physical change

  • Early adulthood (20s–30s): peak physical development.
  • Middle adulthood (40s–50s): lose height, often gain weight; menopause in women (late 40s–early 50s).
  • Late adulthood (60s on): wear and tear; less ability to repair and regenerate.

Biological theories of ageing

TheoryClaim
Cellular-clock theoryCells can divide only about 100 times; telomeres protecting chromosome ends shorten with each division. Predicts a maximum lifespan of about 120 years
Free-radical theoryUnstable oxygen molecules (free radicals) damage DNA and cells, leading to disorders such as cancer
Hormonal stress theoryAn ageing hormonal system lowers resistance to stress; stress hormones linger and raise the risk of heart disease, cancer and diabetes

The ageing brain still grows some new neurons (hippocampus, olfactory bulb), repairs itself as healthy neurons take over from damaged ones, and shows reduced lateralisation (using both hemispheres more), which helps maintain mental abilities.

Cognitive change

  • Early adulthood: idealism gives way to realistic pragmatism.
  • Middle adulthood: peak in vocabulary, verbal memory, inductive reasoning and spatial orientation; numerical ability and perceptual speed decline.
  • Late adulthood: slower processing and memory retrieval; wisdom may grow; strategy training and physical activity help.

Socioemotional change

Erikson's last three stages: intimacy vs isolation, generativity vs stagnation, integrity vs despair. Active, involved older adults are more satisfied and healthier. Socioemotional selectivity theory: aware of limited time, older adults choose fewer, more meaningful relationships. People with positive attitudes to ageing lived on average 7.5 years longer.

sections.title: Psychodynamic perspectives
sections.html:
Personality is a pattern of enduring, distinctive thoughts, emotions and behaviours that characterise the way a person adapts to the world.

Psychodynamic perspectives: personality is mainly unconscious; behaviour has symbolic meanings; early childhood experiences sculpt personality.

Freud (1856–1939)

A Viennese neurologist. His colleague Josef Breuer treated "Anna O.", whose hysteria (physical symptoms with no physical cause) eased when she recovered repressed traumatic memories. This convinced Freud that problems come from the unconscious, a store of feelings and urges we are unaware of, and that symptoms are overdetermined (have several unconscious causes). He saw the sex drive (any organ pleasure) as the main motivator. His iceberg analogy: most of the mind lies below the surface of awareness.

StructureWorks onRole
IdPleasure principle (seek pleasure, avoid pain)Instincts and sexual energy; no contact with reality; fully unconscious
EgoReality principleDeals with the demands of reality; partly conscious
SuperegoMoralityConscience and values; always in conflict with the id

Defence mechanisms

Conflict among id, ego and superego causes anxiety; defence mechanisms reduce it by unconsciously distorting reality. They are not necessarily unhealthy. Repression, pushing unacceptable impulses out of awareness, is the foundation of them all. Others: rationalisation (a reasonable excuse), displacement (redirecting feelings to a safer target), sublimation (channelling urges into acceptable activity), projection (seeing your own impulses in others), reaction formation (acting the opposite), denial and regression (returning to an earlier stage).

Psychosexual stages

StageAgeFocus
Oral0–18 monthsPleasure centres on the mouth
Anal18–36 monthsPleasure from elimination
Phallic3–6 yearsGenitals; Oedipus complex, castration anxiety
Latency6 years–pubertyPsychic 'time-out'; sexual interest repressed
GenitalAdolescence onwardsSexual reawakening; pleasure from someone else

Fixation: staying locked in a stage (e.g. "anal retentive").

Dissenters and revisionists

They argued sexuality is not the force behind personality, early experience is less powerful, and conscious thought and culture matter more.

  • Karen Horney: sociocultural approach; both sexes envy the other's attributes; the need for security, not sex, is primary.
  • Carl Jung: analytical theory; the collective unconscious and archetypes.
  • Alfred Adler: individual psychology; striving for perfection, not pleasure, motivates us.
ContributionsCriticisms
Importance of childhood experienceToo much emphasis on early experience
Development proceeds in stagesToo much faith in the unconscious; too much on sexual instincts
Role of unconscious processesCannot be tested scientifically

sections.title: Humanistic and trait perspectives
sections.html:
Humanistic perspectives

Emphasise the capacity for personal growth and positive human qualities.

  • Abraham Maslow: "third force" psychology; self-actualisation (reaching one's full potential) and peak experiences. Biased because he studied only highly successful people.
  • Carl Rogers: everyone is born good, but others' conditions of worth push us away from our genuine feelings and distort our self-concept. Growth needs unconditional positive regard, empathy and genuineness.

Contributions: self-perception is key; positive side of human nature; conscious experience. Criticisms: too optimistic; may promote self-love and narcissism.

Trait perspectives

A trait is an enduring disposition that leads to characteristic responses; traits are the building blocks of personality, and people differ in how strongly they show each.

  • Gordon Allport: behaviour is consistent across situations; his lexical approach found about 4 500 trait words.
  • W. T. Norman: the five-factor model of broad traits.
Big Five (OCEAN)High scorers are…
OpennessImaginative, curious, open to new experience
ConscientiousnessOrganised, careful, disciplined
ExtraversionSociable, talkative, fun-loving
AgreeablenessKind, trusting, helpful
NeuroticismAnxious, insecure, emotionally unstable

Contributions: traits predict health, thinking, career success and relationships. Criticisms: ignore the situation and the nuances of an individual.

sections.title: Life story, social cognitive and biological perspectives
sections.html:
Personological and life story perspectives

  • Henry Murray: personology, the study of the whole person; motives are largely unconscious; the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT) measures needs for achievement, affiliation and power.
  • Dan McAdams: our life story is our identity; intimacy motivation is a lasting concern for warm relationships.
  • Psychobiography applies personality theory to one person's life.
  • Rich record of experience, but time-consuming (heavy coding), prone to bias and hard to generalise.

Social cognitive perspectives

Emphasise conscious awareness, beliefs, expectations and goals, adding reasoning, self-reflection and interpretation to behaviourist principles.

  • Albert Bandura: reciprocal determinism, in which behaviour, environment and person/cognitive factors all influence each other. Key processes: observational learning, personal control and self-efficacy (belief that you can master a situation).
  • Walter Mischel: situationism, behaviour varies a lot across contexts. His CAPS model: personality is stable over time rather than across situations, and links among thoughts and emotions drive behaviour.
  • Strength: focuses on person–environment interaction and on our control over our environment. Weaknesses: too concerned with change and situations; ignores biology; very specific predictions are hard to generalise.

Biological perspectives

  • Brain damage changes personality (Phineas Gage); brain responses correlate with personality.
  • Eysenck's reticular activation system theory: extraverts and introverts have different baseline arousal (introverts higher, so they avoid extra stimulation).
  • Gray's reinforcement sensitivity theory: a behavioural activation system (reward-seeking, extraversion) and a behavioural inhibition system (punishment-sensitivity, neuroticism).
  • Neurotransmitters: warm caregiving stimulates growth of dopamine receptors, linked to reward-sensitivity and extraversion; low serotonin is linked to negative mood (neuroticism) and aggression.
  • Behaviour genetics: twin studies show substantial genetic influence on the Big Five; most traits involve many genes.
  • Strength: links to animal learning, brain imaging and evolution. Criticism: biology may be an effect of personality, not its cause.
