qs.q: Define psychology and explain each of its three key components. Then describe the attitudes that make psychology a science rather than common sense.
steps: Definition: the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes (2)
Science: systematic methods to observe, describe, predict, explain (2)
Behaviour: what can be directly observed, with an example (2)
Mental processes: thoughts, feelings, motives that are not directly observable, with an example (2)
Critical thinking, scepticism, objectivity and curiosity, each explained with how it protects against common-sense errors (8)
Psychology also studies strengths (positive psychology), not only disorder (2)
qs.ans: A strong answer defines psychology, unpacks all three components with examples, and shows how the four scientific attitudes separate psychology from everyday guessing about people.

qs.q: Compare and contrast structuralism and functionalism. Who founded each, what question did each ask, and what method did each use?
steps: Wundt: structuralism, first lab 1879 in Leipzig, reaction-time experiment showed mental processes can be measured (4)
Structuralism aimed to identify the basic structures/elements of the mind (3)
James: functionalism, the functions and purposes of the mind (3)
Stream of consciousness: mind is flexible and constantly changing; thought is adaptive (3)
Comparison: 'what' vs 'why'; Darwin's influence on functionalism; weakness of introspection (subjective) (4)
qs.ans: Structuralism (Wundt) broke the mind into its parts using introspection; functionalism (James) asked what the mind is for and how it helps us adapt, an idea shaped by Darwin.

qs.q: Describe the seven contemporary approaches to psychology. Use one example of behaviour (such as aggression or anxiety) to show how each approach would explain it differently.
steps: Biological: brain, nervous system, neuroscience (2 + example)
Behavioural: observable behaviour and environment, Watson and Skinner (2 + example)
Psychodynamic: unconscious, drives vs society, childhood, Freud (2 + example)
Humanistic: growth, free will, Rogers and Maslow (2 + example)
Evolutionary: adaptation and natural selection, Buss and Cosmides (2 + example)
Sociocultural: social and cultural context, cross-cultural comparison (2 + example)
qs.ans: Seven approaches, one behaviour: each lens explains a different part of it, which is why psychologists see the approaches as complementary.

qs.q: 'The behavioural and humanistic approaches hold opposite views of human nature.' Discuss.
steps: Behavioural approach: environment shapes observable behaviour; thought processes rejected; Watson and Skinner (5)
Humanistic approach: free will, positive growth, positive qualities; Rogers and Maslow (5)
Point of conflict: determinism (environment controls us) vs free will (we choose) (4)
Point of conflict: observable behaviour only vs inner experience (3)
Balanced conclusion: each explains some behaviour well; approaches are complementary (3)
qs.ans: Behaviourism sees people as shaped by their environment; humanism sees them as choosing and growing. Both views explain part of behaviour, which is why modern psychology keeps both.

qs.group: 3. Careers, specialisations and the mind–body link
qs.q: Describe the main career settings and at least six areas of specialisation in psychology. Then explain how psychology is useful in business, law and education.
steps: Practice/applied, research and teaching; academic, clinical, private, industry, school settings (4)
Business: market research, HR, advertising, sales; business psychology defined (4)
Law: understanding behaviour and decisions, assessment, parole/probation officers (3)
Education: how people learn, individual differences, gifted learners, learning disabilities (3)
qs.ans: Psychology's knowledge of behaviour and its research skills transfer to business, law and education, as well as to clinics and universities.

qs.group: 3. Careers, specialisations and the mind–body link
qs.q: Explain what is meant by the statement 'the mind–body connection is a two-way street'. Give examples of each direction.
steps: Mind affects body: stress, worry or optimism changing physical health, with example (4)
Body affects mind: illness, sleep, exercise or nutrition changing mood and thinking, with example (4)
Link to health psychology and wellness (2)
qs.ans: Mental states change physical health, and physical states change mental health; health psychology studies both directions.

qs.q: Describe the five steps of the scientific method. Use one research question of your own (for example, 'Does sleep affect exam performance?') to illustrate each step.
steps: Science as a method; role of theory (2)
Hypothesis: testable prediction from theory, not yet a fact (3)
Research: design, participants, data collection, statistical analysis (3)
Evaluate: never ends, journals, conferences, meta-analysis (3)
Own example carried through every step (3)
qs.ans: The method moves from observation to a testable hypothesis, to empirical research, to conclusions, to ongoing evaluation; replication and meta-analysis decide whether a result holds.

qs.q: What is an operational definition, and why is it essential in psychological research? Give operational definitions for two variables, such as happiness and aggression.
steps: Definition: how a variable will be observed and measured (2)
Removes grey areas and confusion; makes replication possible (3)
Two clear operational definitions, e.g. Satisfaction with Life Scale score; number of hits on a doll (4)
Note that different definitions can produce different findings (1)
qs.ans: Operational definitions turn vague ideas into measurable variables, so studies can be checked and repeated.

qs.q: Compare descriptive, correlational and experimental research. For each, state its goal, describe its methods and explain its main limitation.
steps: Descriptive: goal, observation/surveys/case studies, cannot explain why (6)
Correlational: goal, r from −1 to +1, positive vs negative, prediction (6)
Experimental: IV, DV, experimental and control groups, random assignment, causation (7)
Comparison table or summary of when to use each (3)
qs.ans: Descriptive research says what happens, correlational research says what goes together, and only experiments with random assignment can show what causes what.

qs.q: 'Correlation does not equal causation.' Explain this statement, including the third variable problem, and discuss why correlational research is still valuable.
steps: Correlation shows a relationship, not which causes which (3)
Direction problem: either variable could cause the other (2)
Third variable problem with a worked example (4)
Value: prediction; studying variables that cannot ethically be manipulated, e.g. prenatal alcohol (4)
Longitudinal designs as a partial answer (2)
qs.ans: Two variables moving together does not tell us that one causes the other, but correlations still predict and let us study things we could never ethically manipulate.

qs.q: Design an experiment to test whether playing violent video games increases aggression. Identify the independent and dependent variables, the groups, and explain how you would control for bias.
steps: IV: violent vs non-violent game; DV operationally defined aggression (4)
Experimental and control groups; random assignment and why (4)
Experimenter bias, demand characteristics, participant bias, placebo (4)
Internal and external validity, ethics (debriefing, consent) (4)
qs.ans: A sound design randomly assigns players to violent or non-violent games, measures operationally defined aggression, and uses a double-blind procedure to keep expectations out of the results.

qs.q: Distinguish between reliability and validity. Explain internal and external validity, and discuss the main sources of bias in experiments.
steps: Validity: measures what it intends; reliable ≠ valid (3)
Experimenter bias, demand characteristics, participant bias, placebo effect (6)
qs.ans: Reliable findings repeat; valid findings are accurate. Bias from either side threatens validity, and double-blind designs guard against it.

qs.q: Explain the difference between a population and a sample, and between representative and random samples. Then compare laboratory research with naturalistic observation.
steps: Representative vs biased sample; random sample (4)
Setting does not determine the research type (2)
qs.ans: Good samples mirror the population; labs offer control but less realism, natural settings the reverse, and any design can run in either.

qs.q: Distinguish between descriptive and inferential statistics. Explain the mean, median, mode, range and standard deviation, and what it means for a result to be statistically significant.
steps: Mean, median, mode with a small example (4)
Significance: p < 0.05, p < 0.01; chance vs real difference (3)
qs.ans: Descriptive statistics summarise; inferential statistics test whether a difference is real. p < 0.05 means less than a 5% chance it arose by chance.

qs.group: 7. Research ethics and being a wise consumer
qs.q: Discuss the ethical principles that guide psychological research with humans and animals.
steps: IRB and APA guidelines; researcher bias (3)
Deception: when allowed and how handled (3)
Animal research: benefits, how common, standards of care (5)
qs.ans: Participants' rights are protected by consent, confidentiality, debriefing and limits on deception; animals are protected by standards of care.

qs.group: 7. Research ethics and being a wise consumer
qs.q: How can you become a wise consumer of psychological information in the media? Use examples.
steps: Expressive-writing research as an example of good evidence (3)
qs.ans: Read research claims carefully: check the source, the sample, the design and whether other studies agree before accepting a headline.

qs.group: 8. The nervous system and its divisions
qs.q: Describe the organisation of the human nervous system, from the central and peripheral nervous systems down to the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions. Explain what each division does.
steps: Nervous system as electrochemical communication system (2)
Sympathetic: arousal for stress; parasympathetic: calming (5)
qs.ans: The CNS processes; the PNS connects. The PNS splits into somatic and autonomic systems, and the autonomic system into sympathetic (arouse) and parasympathetic (calm).

qs.group: 8. The nervous system and its divisions
qs.q: Explain the four characteristics of the nervous system that allow it to direct behaviour.
steps: Integration: each neuron talks to about 10 000 others (3)
qs.ans: Complexity, integration, plasticity and electrochemical transmission let the nervous system process information and adapt.

qs.group: 9. Neurons, the neural impulse and neurotransmitters
qs.q: With the help of a labelled diagram, describe the structure of a neuron and explain how a neural impulse travels along the axon.
steps: Labelled diagram: cell body, dendrites, axon, myelin, terminal buttons (5)
Functions of each part; myelin and multiple sclerosis (5)
Depolarisation, sodium in, potassium out; action potential (5)
qs.ans: A neuron receives on its dendrites, integrates in the cell body and fires an all-or-none action potential down its myelinated axon as ions cross the membrane.
qs.hint: Draw the neuron first, then follow the charge from resting to firing.

qs.group: 9. Neurons, the neural impulse and neurotransmitters
qs.q: Explain synaptic transmission. Then discuss at least five neurotransmitters, their functions and the disorders associated with them, and explain how drugs act on synapses.
steps: Five neurotransmitters with functions and disorders (10)
Agonists vs antagonists with examples, e.g. Prozac (4)
qs.ans: The electrical signal becomes chemical at the synapse; each neurotransmitter has its own job and its own disorders, and drugs work by mimicking or blocking them.

qs.group: 9. Neurons, the neural impulse and neurotransmitters
qs.q: What are mirror neurons and glial cells? Explain their importance.
steps: Mirror neurons fire when acting and when watching the same action (3)
Role in imitation, empathy, understanding others (3)
Glial cells: support, nutrition, roughly as many as neurons (3)
Neurons do most of the processing (1)
qs.ans: Mirror neurons link watching and doing; glia support the neurons that do the processing.

qs.group: 10. Studying the brain and its structures
qs.q: Describe the main techniques used to study the brain, and evaluate what each can and cannot tell us.
steps: MRI and fMRI: structure vs function (5)
qs.ans: Each technique answers a different question: lesions and TMS link areas to behaviour, EEG tracks electrical activity, CT and MRI show structure, and PET and fMRI show activity.

qs.group: 10. Studying the brain and its structures
qs.q: Describe the structures and functions of the hindbrain, midbrain and forebrain.
steps: Development from a neural tube into three parts (2)
Hindbrain: medulla, cerebellum, pons, brain stem (6)
Midbrain: relay for eyes and ears, reticular formation, substantia nigra and Parkinson's (5)
Forebrain: amygdala, hippocampus, thalamus, basal ganglia, hypothalamus (7)
qs.ans: Survival functions sit low in the hindbrain, relays in the midbrain, and emotion, memory and regulation in the forebrain.

qs.group: 11. The cerebral cortex and the two hemispheres
qs.q: Discuss the four lobes of the cerebral cortex and their functions. Use the case of Phineas Gage to show what happens when the frontal lobe is damaged.
steps: Occipital, temporal, frontal, parietal with functions (8)
Gage: accident, left frontal damage, personality change (5)
What this shows about frontal lobe and personality (3)
qs.ans: Each lobe has its own work; Gage's change in personality after frontal damage shows the frontal lobe's role in personality and planning.

qs.group: 11. The cerebral cortex and the two hemispheres
qs.q: Explain hemispheric specialisation. Discuss the roles of the left and right hemispheres, Broca's and Wernicke's areas, and what split-brain research has shown.
steps: Left hemisphere: language functions; right side of the body (4)
Right hemisphere: non-verbal, spatial, faces, emotion; left side of the body (4)
Corpus callosum; split-brain case W. J. (5)
qs.ans: The left hemisphere specialises in language and the right in non-verbal processing; the corpus callosum lets them work as one, as split-brain cases show.

qs.group: 11. The cerebral cortex and the two hemispheres
qs.q: Explain the somatosensory, motor and association cortex, including Penfield's research and the fusiform face area.
steps: Somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe (2)
Motor cortex in the frontal lobe (2)
qs.ans: Sensation and movement are mapped point-to-point onto the cortex, while the large association cortex integrates them for thought.

qs.q: Describe the endocrine system and the functions of its main glands. How does it differ from the nervous system?
qs.ans: The endocrine system uses hormones in the blood to regulate the body more slowly than nerves; the pituitary controls the other glands.

qs.q: Discuss how genes and the environment together shape behaviour. Refer to behaviour genetics, twin studies, genotype and phenotype.
steps: Behaviour genetics and twin studies: identical vs fraternal (5)
Gene expression influenced by environment, with example such as height (4)
qs.ans: Genes set possibilities and the environment shapes how they are expressed; twin studies estimate how much each contributes.

qs.q: Explain brain plasticity and the ways a damaged brain can repair itself.
steps: Recovery depends on age and extent of damage (2)
Collateral sprouting, substitution of function, neurogenesis, grafts (6)
qs.ans: The brain can rewire, take over functions, grow neurons and accept grafts; younger brains with less damage recover best.

qs.group: 13. What learning is, and classical conditioning
qs.q: Define learning. Using Pavlov's experiment, explain classical conditioning, identifying the UCS, UCR, NS, CS and CR, and the conditions needed for acquisition.
steps: Five terms defined and applied to the dogs (8)
qs.ans: Pairing a neutral bell with food (UCS) until the bell alone produces salivation turns it into a CS producing a CR; contiguity and contingency make the pairing work.

qs.group: 13. What learning is, and classical conditioning
qs.q: Explain generalisation, discrimination, extinction, spontaneous recovery and renewal in classical conditioning, with examples.
steps: Discrimination and how it is learned (3)
qs.ans: Learned responses spread to similar stimuli, can be narrowed, fade without the UCS, and can return after time or in a new context.

qs.group: 13. What learning is, and classical conditioning
qs.q: Discuss how classical conditioning applies to everyday life. Refer to phobias (Little Albert), counterconditioning and at least three other applications.
steps: Little Albert: rat as CS, noise as UCS, fear as CR (5)
Three of: placebo, immune/endocrine, taste aversion, advertising, drug habituation, each explained (6)
qs.ans: Classical conditioning explains how fears, tastes, adverts and even drug tolerance are learned, and counterconditioning shows they can be unlearned.

qs.q: Explain operant conditioning. Distinguish positive and negative reinforcement from positive and negative punishment, giving an example of each.
steps: Clear statement that negative reinforcement increases behaviour (2)
qs.ans: Reinforcement increases behaviour and punishment decreases it; 'positive' adds a stimulus and 'negative' removes one.

qs.q: Describe the four schedules of partial reinforcement and explain which produces behaviour most resistant to extinction. Use real-life examples.
steps: Variable interval with example (fishing, pop quizzes) (3)
Variable schedules, especially VR, most resistant to extinction; why (5)
qs.ans: Ratio schedules count responses and interval schedules count time; unpredictable (variable) schedules, especially variable ratio, keep behaviour going longest.

qs.q: Discuss the controversy over punishment, especially corporal punishment. What alternatives does operant conditioning suggest?
steps: How common it is; correlational evidence (4)
Alternatives: reinforcement, negative punishment, applied behaviour analysis (6)
qs.ans: Physical punishment is common but linked to problems; reinforcing desired behaviour and behaviour modification are better tools.

qs.q: Compare classical and operant conditioning.
steps: Both associative learning; contingency in both (3)
Example of the same situation explained by each (5)
qs.ans: Classical conditioning links two stimuli to shape involuntary responses; operant conditioning links behaviour to consequences to shape voluntary actions.

qs.q: Explain Bandura's observational learning and its four processes. How does it challenge strict behaviourism?
steps: Relies on mental processes, unlike behaviourism (4)
qs.ans: We learn by watching, but only if we attend, remember, can reproduce and have a reason to act, which shows that thinking matters in learning.

qs.q: Discuss the role of cognitive factors in learning, referring to Tolman's work and Köhler's insight learning.
steps: Evaluation: learning is more than stimulus–response (5)
qs.ans: Tolman and Köhler showed that organisms form mental maps, learn without reward and solve problems by insight: cognition matters in learning.

qs.group: 16. Biological, cultural and psychological factors in learning
qs.q: Discuss biological, cultural and psychological factors that limit or shape learning.
steps: Culture: how and what we learn (3)
qs.ans: Biology makes some learning easy and some hard, culture decides what we meet, and mindset decides how much we keep trying.

qs.q: What are concepts? Explain why they are important and describe the prototype model.
steps: Concepts as mental categories with examples (2)
Prototype model: tend to vs must possess (3)
qs.ans: Concepts organise experience so we can generalise, associate, remember and react; the prototype model explains how unusual members still fit.

qs.q: Describe the steps in problem solving and the strategies people use. Discuss the obstacles that can block solutions.
steps: Fixation and functional fixedness with examples (5)
qs.ans: Good problem solving frames the problem well, picks the right strategy, checks the answer and keeps rethinking; fixation and functional fixedness get in the way.

qs.group: 18. Reasoning, decision making, and critical and creative thinking
qs.q: Distinguish between inductive and deductive reasoning, and between System I and System II thinking, with examples.
qs.ans: Induction builds general rules from cases; deduction applies rules to cases. System I is fast and intuitive, System II slow and analytical.

qs.group: 18. Reasoning, decision making, and critical and creative thinking
qs.q: Discuss five biases and heuristics that affect decision making. How can critical thinking reduce their effect?
steps: Critical thinking: mindfulness, open-mindedness, System II (3)
qs.ans: Shortcuts make decisions fast but biased; slowing down to weigh evidence reduces their pull.

qs.group: 18. Reasoning, decision making, and critical and creative thinking
qs.q: Explain the difference between divergent and convergent thinking. Describe the characteristics of creative thinkers and how mood affects thinking.
qs.ans: Creativity relies on divergent thinking and on flexible, motivated, risk-taking people; good moods favour creativity and bad moods careful logic.

qs.q: How is intelligence measured? Explain mental age, IQ, the normal distribution and the main intelligence tests, and discuss cultural bias in testing.
steps: Binet: MA vs CA; Stern's IQ formula with a worked example (5)
qs.ans: IQ compares mental to chronological age, and scores fall on a bell curve around 100, but tests can be culturally biased, which culture-fair tests try to fix.
qs.hint: Show the formula with numbers: MA 12, CA 10 → IQ 120.

qs.q: Compare Sternberg's triarchic theory with Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences. Do they improve on a single g factor?
qs.ans: Both theories say intelligence has many forms, unlike a single g; Sternberg keeps three broad abilities, Gardner nine more specific ones.

qs.q: Discuss genetic and environmental influences on intelligence, and describe the extremes of intelligence.
steps: Intellectual disability: IQ < 70, adaptive behaviour, organic vs cultural-familial, levels (6)
qs.ans: Genes and environment both shape intelligence; the Flynn effect shows environment can raise scores quickly.

qs.q: Describe the five rule systems of language and explain what is meant by infinite generativity.
steps: Phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics, each with an example (10)
qs.ans: Five rule systems, from sounds to social use, let a finite set of symbols produce endless meaningful sentences.

qs.q: 'Language determines thought.' Discuss this claim, and explain biological and environmental influences on language.
steps: Evidence that language influences rather than determines thought; two-way relationship (4)
qs.ans: Language shapes thought without fully determining it; language itself grows from both biology and experience, as Genie's case shows.

qs.group: 21. Studying development, prenatal and infant growth
qs.q: Define development and its three levels. Compare cross-sectional and longitudinal research designs, and explain the nature–nurture debate.
steps: Definition: continuity and change; physical, cognitive, socioemotional (4)
Nature vs nurture; the active developer (5)
qs.ans: Development is lifelong change on three levels; it is studied across or within cohorts, and it results from nature, nurture and the person's own choices.

qs.group: 21. Studying development, prenatal and infant growth
qs.q: Describe the three periods of prenatal development and discuss how teratogens can affect the developing child.
qs.ans: Prenatal development moves from zygote to embryo to fetus; teratogens do most harm when an organ is forming, but genes and later care change the outcome.

qs.q: Describe Piaget's theory of cognitive development, including schemas, assimilation, accommodation and the four stages. Evaluate the theory.
steps: Four stages with ages and key features (10)
Evaluation: object permanence at 4 months, stages vs small steps, culture (6)
qs.ans: Piaget showed children think differently from adults and pass through four stages, but later research shows infants know more, earlier, and that culture matters.

qs.group: 23. Temperament, attachment, Erikson, parenting and moral development
qs.q: Explain infant attachment, referring to Harlow's monkey studies and Ainsworth's Strange Situation. Why is attachment important?
qs.ans: Harlow showed comfort, not food, drives attachment; Ainsworth showed how to measure it. Secure attachment lays a foundation for later relationships.

qs.group: 23. Temperament, attachment, Erikson, parenting and moral development
qs.q: Discuss Erikson's eight psychosocial stages of development.
steps: Lifelong development; crisis at each stage (3)
Adolescent stage: identity vs identity confusion (3)
qs.ans: Erikson saw life as eight crises, from trust in infancy to integrity in old age; resolving each builds a strength for the next.

qs.group: 23. Temperament, attachment, Erikson, parenting and moral development
qs.q: Describe the four parenting styles and their outcomes for children. Which parenting strategies support moral development, according to Kohlberg's work?
qs.ans: Authoritative parenting, warm with firm limits, gives the best outcomes and also supports moral growth through reasoning and modelling.

qs.group: 23. Temperament, attachment, Erikson, parenting and moral development
qs.q: What is temperament? Describe the main ways of classifying it.
steps: Chess and Thomas: easy, difficult, slow-to-warm-up (4)
qs.ans: Temperament is a child's characteristic style of responding, an early foundation for later personality.

qs.q: Discuss the physical, cognitive and socioemotional changes of adolescence. Include brain development and Marcia's identity statuses.
steps: Amygdala early, prefrontal cortex late; risk-taking (5)
Erikson identity vs confusion; Marcia's four statuses (6)
qs.ans: Adolescents mature physically before the brain's control centre catches up; they think abstractly but egocentrically, and work towards an identity through exploration and commitment.

qs.group: 25. Emerging adulthood, adult development and ageing
qs.q: Describe the physical and cognitive changes that occur in early, middle and late adulthood, and discuss three biological theories of ageing.
steps: Cognitive change across adulthood; the ageing brain (6)
qs.ans: Physical peaks come early and decline later; three theories explain ageing as cell limits, free-radical damage and stress hormones, while many mental abilities peak in middle age.

qs.group: 25. Emerging adulthood, adult development and ageing
qs.q: How do older adults maintain well-being? Discuss socioemotional selectivity theory and Erikson's later stages.
qs.ans: Older adults thrive when active and close to people they value, and when they look back on life with integrity rather than despair.

qs.q: Describe Freud's psychoanalytic theory of personality. Discuss the structure of personality (id, ego, superego) and the role of defence mechanisms.
steps: Psychodynamic view: unconscious, symbolic meanings, childhood (3)
Anna O. and hysteria; the unconscious; iceberg analogy (4)
Id, ego and superego with principles (6)
Anxiety from conflict; defence mechanisms defined (3)
Repression plus at least three other mechanisms with examples (6)
qs.ans: Freud saw personality as a battle between id, ego and superego, mostly below awareness, with defence mechanisms distorting reality to keep anxiety down.

qs.q: Explain Freud's psychosexual stages of development, including fixation. How did Horney, Jung and Adler revise Freud's ideas?
steps: Oral, anal, phallic, latency, genital with ages (8)
qs.ans: Freud's five stages centre pleasure on different body zones; his followers kept the unconscious but swapped sex for security, archetypes or striving for perfection.

qs.q: Critically evaluate the psychodynamic perspective on personality.
steps: Criticisms: early experience, unconscious, sexual instincts (6)
qs.ans: Psychodynamic theory gave psychology the importance of childhood and the unconscious, but its claims are hard to test and overemphasise sex and early experience.

qs.q: Compare the humanistic theories of Maslow and Rogers, and evaluate the humanistic perspective.
steps: Maslow: third force, self-actualisation, peak experiences, bias (5)
Rogers: born good, conditions of worth, self-concept (5)
qs.ans: Maslow and Rogers both stressed growth: Maslow through self-actualisation, Rogers through unconditional positive regard. The approach is uplifting but arguably too optimistic.

qs.q: Explain the trait perspective on personality, describing Allport's work and the five-factor model. Evaluate the approach.
qs.ans: Trait theory describes people by stable dispositions, summed up in the Big Five (OCEAN); it predicts real outcomes but neglects situations.

qs.group: 28. Life story, social cognitive and biological perspectives
qs.q: Explain Bandura's and Mischel's social cognitive perspectives on personality.
steps: Social cognitive emphasis on beliefs and goals (2)
Reciprocal determinism with a diagram or example (5)
qs.ans: Bandura sees personality emerging from the interplay of person, behaviour and environment; Mischel shows behaviour varies by situation but is stable over time.

qs.group: 28. Life story, social cognitive and biological perspectives
qs.q: Discuss biological perspectives on personality, including Eysenck, Gray, neurotransmitters and behaviour genetics.
steps: Eysenck: arousal in extraverts vs introverts (4)
qs.ans: Biology shapes personality through brain arousal systems, neurotransmitters and genes, though biology may also be shaped by personality.

qs.group: 28. Life story, social cognitive and biological perspectives
qs.q: Describe Murray's personology and McAdams's life story approach. What are their strengths and weaknesses?
steps: TAT and needs for achievement, affiliation, power (3)
McAdams: life story as identity; intimacy motivation (4)
qs.ans: These approaches study the whole person through life stories: rich but time-consuming, prone to bias and hard to generalise.

qs.q: Describe and evaluate the main methods of personality assessment.
steps: Empirically keyed tests and the MMPI (4)
Projective: Rorschach and TAT; reliability and validity (5)
qs.ans: Self-report inventories such as the MMPI and NEO-PI-R are the most supported; the MBTI and projective tests are popular but weaker on reliability and validity.

qs.q: Choose one behaviour (for example, a student who procrastinates). Explain it from the psychodynamic, humanistic, trait, social cognitive and biological perspectives on personality.
qs.ans: Each perspective highlights a different cause; a complete explanation draws on several.
